subject: Mathematics
title: Arun's Friendship Rules
hook: Can friendship be a function? Arun discovers relations and functions through his boarding school friend groups.

characters.name: Coach Vikram
characters.role: Sports coach, explains domain and range

slides.title: Relations and Functions
slides.storyContext: Arun arrives at boarding school and notices patterns in how students connect.

slides.title: The Friendship Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arun's dorm has 4 students: Arun (A), Priya (P), Rohan (R), and Zara (Z). Arun notices: A is friends with P and R; P is friends with A and Z; R is friends with A; Z is friends with P. He asks Coach Vikram if this friendship pattern follows a rule.

slides.title: What is a Relation?
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram explains: A relation is ANY set of ordered pairs. Friendship from person X to person Y is (X, Y).

points.label: Definition
points.text: A relation R from set A to set B is a subset of A × B (the Cartesian product).

points.label: Example in the story
points.text: Friendship relation = {(A,P), (A,R), (P,A), (P,Z), (R,A), (Z,P)}. Not every pair is friends — (A,Z) is NOT in the relation.

slides.inSimpleWords: A relation is a connection or pairing between things. It doesn't have to follow a strict rule — any subset of pairs works.

slides.title: Domain and Range
slides.storyContext: Coach asks: Who are all the students doing the friending (the 'from' side)? Who are all the students being friended (the 'to' side)?

points.label: Domain
points.text: The set of all first elements (inputs): {A, P, R, Z}. Who are the ones doing the action?

points.label: Range
points.text: The set of all second elements (outputs): {A, P, R, Z}. Who are the ones receiving the action?

example.problem: For the relation R = {(A,P), (A,R), (P,A), (P,Z), (R,A), (Z,P)}, find domain and range.
example.solution: Domain = {A, P, R, Z}. Range = {P, R, A, Z} = {A, P, R, Z}.

slides.inSimpleWords: Domain = who sends the relation. Range = who receives it.

slides.title: What is a Function?
slides.storyContext: Arun realizes: in the classroom, EVERY student has EXACTLY ONE class teacher. This is different from friendship — some have no friends, some have many, but EVERY student has ONE teacher. Priya calls this a function.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A function f: A → B is a special relation where every element of A maps to EXACTLY ONE element of B. No element is left out; no element maps to two different values.

points.label: Vertical Line Test
points.text: If a relation is shown as a graph, a vertical line crosses it at most once ⟹ it's a function.

example.problem: Is f = {(A,P), (A,R), (P,Z), (R,A), (Z,P)} a function from {A,P,R,Z} to itself?
example.solution: No. A maps to both P and R (two outputs). In a function, A must map to exactly one value.

slides.inSimpleWords: A function is a relation with a strict rule: each input has ONE and ONLY ONE output.

slides.title: Types of Functions
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram introduces three important types through school scenarios.

points.label: One-to-one (Injective)
points.text: Different students get different class teachers. No two students share the same teacher.

points.label: Onto (Surjective)
points.text: Every teacher in the school teaches at least one student. No teacher is left without a class.

points.label: Bijective (One-to-one AND Onto)
points.text: Perfect pairing: each student has one unique teacher, and each teacher has one unique student. This is reversible (has an inverse).

slides.inSimpleWords: Injective = no collisions (different inputs → different outputs). Surjective = all outputs are used. Bijective = perfect match both ways.

slides.title: Inverse Function
slides.storyContext: If teacher Ms. Sharma teaches Arun (f: Arun → Ms. Sharma), then the inverse asks: which student does Ms. Sharma teach? (f⁻¹: Ms. Sharma → Arun). Only bijective functions have inverses.

points.label: Inverse exists only for bijective functions
points.text: f⁻¹ exists ⟺ f is both injective and surjective.

points.label: Property
points.text: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x and f⁻¹(f(x)) = x for all x in the domain.

example.problem: If f(x) = 2x + 3, find f⁻¹(x).

slides.inSimpleWords: The inverse function reverses the direction: if f takes input to output, f⁻¹ takes the output back to the original input.

slides.title: Composition of Functions
slides.storyContext: Arun realizes: first, the class teacher assigns students to projects (f). Then, the project groups go to different labs (g). The combined route (student → project group → lab) is the composition g∘f.

points.label: (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x))
points.text: Apply f first, then g to the result. Order matters: g∘f ≠ f∘g usually.

example.problem: If f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, find (g∘f)(3) and (f∘g)(3).
example.solution: (g∘f)(3) = g(f(3)) = g(4) = 8. (f∘g)(3) = f(g(3)) = f(6) = 7. Different answers — order matters!

slides.inSimpleWords: Composition chains functions: do f first, then g. Like getting dressed: socks (f), then shoes (g). Can't do it backwards the same way.

slides.title: Challenge: Verify Bijective and Find Inverse
slides.storyContext: Priya gives Arun a puzzle: The dorm assigns each student a unique room number. f(x) = 2x − 1 maps x ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4} to room numbers. Is this a bijection from {1, 2, 3, 4} to {1, 3, 5, 7}? If yes, find the inverse.

example.problem: Show that f(x) = 2x − 1 is bijective on the given sets and find f⁻¹.
example.solution: f(1) = 1, f(2) = 3, f(3) = 5, f(4) = 7. All outputs are distinct (injective) and all outputs {1,3,5,7} are covered (surjective). So bijective. Inverse: f⁻¹(y) = (y + 1)/2. Verify: f⁻¹(1) = 1, f⁻¹(3) = 2, f⁻¹(5) = 3, f⁻¹(7) = 4. ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Bijective means perfect one-to-one pairing with all outputs used. If so, you can always reverse it.

slides.title: What Arun Learned
slides.storyContext: Arun now understands how friendships differ from assigned class roles.

points.text: A relation is ANY set of ordered pairs; a function is a relation where each input has exactly one output.
Domain = set of all inputs; Range = set of all outputs.
Injective (one-to-one) = different inputs give different outputs. Surjective (onto) = all outputs are used.
Bijective = both injective and surjective; only bijective functions have inverses.
Composition g∘f means: apply f first, then g. Order matters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Relations are flexible pairings. Functions are strict: one input → one output. Some functions can be reversed (bijections); most cannot.

subject: Mathematics
title: Kavya's Angle Hunt
hook: Kavya's drone footage reveals angles hidden in nature. She learns to find angles using inverse trig functions.

slides.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
slides.storyContext: Kavya's drone captures a temple tower casting a shadow. She knows the height and shadow length — but needs to find the angle of elevation. Arjun introduces inverse trig functions.

slides.title: The Temple Tower Mystery
slides.storyContext: Kavya's drone spots Meenakshi Temple. The tower is 50 meters tall and casts a 50-meter shadow on flat ground. What is the angle of elevation from the shadow tip to the tower top? If sin(θ) = y, then arcsin(y) gives θ back. That's the inverse.

slides.title: What are Inverse Trig Functions?
slides.storyContext: Arjun explains: Trig functions take an angle and give a ratio (e.g., sin(30°) = 0.5). Inverse trig functions take a ratio and give back an angle.

points.label: arcsin (or sin⁻¹)
points.text: If sin(θ) = y, then arcsin(y) = θ. Returns angles in [−π/2, π/2].

points.label: arccos (or cos⁻¹)
points.text: If cos(θ) = y, then arccos(y) = θ. Returns angles in [0, π].

points.label: arctan (or tan⁻¹)
points.text: If tan(θ) = y, then arctan(y) = θ. Returns angles in (−π/2, π/2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Inverse trig functions reverse the direction: instead of angle → ratio, they do ratio → angle.

slides.title: Domain and Range of Inverse Functions
slides.storyContext: Nisha teaches Kavya: each inverse trig function has a specific range (where it outputs angles). This ensures it's a true function (one-to-one).

points.label: arcsin: domain [−1, 1], range [−π/2, π/2]
points.text: For any y between −1 and 1, arcsin(y) gives an angle between −90° and 90°.

points.label: arccos: domain [−1, 1], range [0, π]
points.text: For any y between −1 and 1, arccos(y) gives an angle between 0° and 180°.

points.label: arctan: domain (−∞, ∞), range (−π/2, π/2)
points.text: For any real number y, arctan(y) gives an angle between −90° and 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each inverse has limits: sine/cosine/tangent values must be in a specific range for the inverse to work.

slides.title: The Temple Tower Problem Solved
slides.storyContext: Kavya applies arctan: tower height = 50 m, shadow = 50 m. So tan(θ) = 50/50 = 1. What angle has tan = 1?

points.label: Setup
points.text: tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent = height/shadow = 50/50 = 1.

points.label: Apply arctan
points.text: θ = arctan(1) = π/4 radians = 45°.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The angle of elevation from shadow tip to tower top is 45°.

example.problem: A ladder leans against a wall. The ladder is 10 m long, and its base is 6 m from the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

slides.inSimpleWords: Know the ratio (sine, cosine, or tangent value), use the inverse function to find the angle.

slides.title: Inverse Cotangent, Secant, Cosecant
slides.storyContext: Nisha mentions three more inverse functions, less common but important for full coverage.

points.label: arccot: domain (−∞, ∞), range (0, π)
points.text: If cot(θ) = y, then arccot(y) = θ.

points.label: arcsec: domain (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞), range [0, π] \ {π/2}
points.text: If sec(θ) = y, then arcsec(y) = θ.

points.label: arccsc: domain (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞), range [−π/2, π/2] \ {0}
points.text: If csc(θ) = y, then arccsc(y) = θ.

slides.inSimpleWords: These are less common but follow the same idea: ratio → angle, with specific ranges to ensure one-to-one mapping.

image.alt: Inverse Cotangent, Secant, Cosecant — Inverse Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Key Identities
slides.storyContext: Arjun lists formulas Kavya will use often when solving problems involving inverse trig.

points.label: arcsin(x) + arccos(x) = π/2
points.text: For any x ∈ [−1, 1].

points.label: arctan(x) + arccot(x) = π/2
points.text: For any x ∈ ℝ.

points.label: sin(arcsin(x)) = x
points.text: For x ∈ [−1, 1]. The function and its inverse cancel.

slides.inSimpleWords: These identities let you rewrite and simplify equations involving inverse trig functions.

slides.title: Bridge Construction Problem
slides.storyContext: Nisha's company plans a foot-bridge over a river. From point A on one bank, the angle of elevation to the top of a pole on the opposite bank is 30°. The horizontal distance is 20 m. Find the pole height.

points.label: Given
points.text: Angle of elevation θ = 30°, horizontal distance = 20 m.

points.label: Setup
points.text: tan(30°) = height / 20.

example.problem: Find the pole height.
example.solution: tan(30°) = 1/√3 ≈ 0.577. Height = 20 × tan(30°) = 20 / √3 = 20√3 / 3 ≈ 11.55 m. Alternatively: if height = h, then 30° = arctan(h/20), so h = 20 · tan(arctan(h/20)). Direct: h = 20 · tan(30°) ≈ 11.55 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you know an angle and one side, trig gets you the other. When you know sides and need the angle, inverse trig is your tool.

image.alt: Bridge Construction Problem — Inverse Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-Angle Problem
slides.storyContext: Kavya's drone measures angles from two locations. From point P, the angle of elevation to a cloud is arctan(2). From point Q (30 m closer), it's arctan(3). How high is the cloud?

example.problem: Solve for the cloud height h.
example.solution: From P: tan(θ₁) = 2, so h / d = 2, giving h = 2d. From Q (30 m closer): tan(θ₂) = 3, so h / (d − 30) = 3. Substituting: 2d / (d − 30) = 3. Solving: 2d = 3d − 90, so d = 90 m. Thus h = 2(90) = 180 m. Verify: from Q, h / (90 − 30) = 180 / 60 = 3. ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine two inverse trig observations to set up a system and solve for unknowns.

slides.title: What Kavya Learned
slides.storyContext: Kavya now reads angles from ratios, a skill that applies to drone navigation, surveying, and architecture.

points.text: Inverse trig functions reverse trig: given a ratio (sine, cosine, tangent), find the angle.
Each inverse has a specific range to ensure it's a true function (bijective on its domain).
arcsin domain [−1,1] → angle [−π/2, π/2]; arccos domain [−1,1] → angle [0, π]; arctan domain ℝ → angle (−π/2, π/2).
Key identity: arcsin(x) + arccos(x) = π/2.
Applications: finding angles of elevation/depression, surveying, architecture, navigation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inverse trig functions are your tool when you know ratios and need angles. Essential for real-world geometry.

image.alt: What Kavya Learned — Inverse Trigonometric Functions

subject: Mathematics
title: Rohan's Sports Statistics
hook: Rohan organizes cricket team statistics using matrices, discovering patterns in wins, losses, and runs.

characters.name: Rohan
characters.role: Cricket team captain and stats enthusiast

slides.title: Matrices
slides.storyContext: Rohan's state cricket team needs to organize statistics for 4 matches across 3 categories (runs, wickets, boundaries). Matrices become his organizational tool.

slides.title: The Match Statistics Table
slides.storyContext: Rohan creates a table: Match 1, 2, 3, 4 (columns) × Runs, Wickets, Boundaries (rows). He fills in numbers. Simran says: that's a matrix. Matrices organize data in rows and columns, making calculations easy.

slides.title: What is a Matrix?
slides.storyContext: Simran explains: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns.

points.label: Notation
points.text: A matrix A with m rows and n columns is denoted A_{m×n} or A_{mn}. Element a_{ij} is in row i, column j.

points.label: Square matrix
points.text: If m = n (same number of rows and columns), it's square. Special matrices include identity (main diagonal = 1) and zero (all 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: A matrix is just an organized table of numbers. Rows go horizontal, columns go vertical.

slides.title: Types of Matrices
slides.storyContext: Rohan and Simran identify special matrix types they'll encounter.

points.label: Row matrix
points.text: Only one row, e.g. [1 2 3] is 1×3.

points.label: Column matrix
points.text: Only one column, e.g. [1; 2; 3] is 3×1.

points.label: Diagonal matrix
points.text: Non-zero elements only on the main diagonal, others zero. Diagonal = {a_{11}, a_{22}, a_{33}, ...}.

points.label: Transpose A^T
points.text: Swap rows and columns. If A is m×n, A^T is n×m. Element (i,j) becomes (j,i).

example.solution: A^T = [[1 4], [2 5], [3 6]]. A is 2×3; A^T is 3×2. Rows become columns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Special matrices include row/column (thin shapes), diagonals (marked elements on the main diagonal), and transposes (flipped rows/columns).

slides.title: Matrix Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Rohan compares two tournaments' statistics (each a 3×4 matrix). He adds matrices element-by-element to get combined stats.

points.label: Addition
points.text: Only matrices of same size can be added. (A + B)_{ij} = A_{ij} + B_{ij}.

points.label: Subtraction
points.text: Likewise: (A − B)_{ij} = A_{ij} − B_{ij}.

points.label: Properties
points.text: Commutative: A + B = B + A. Associative: (A + B) + C = A + (B + C). Additive identity: A + O = A (O is zero matrix).

example.problem: Tournament 1: [[150, 160], [5, 4]]. Tournament 2: [[155, 145], [6, 5]]. Find total stats A + B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add matrices by adding corresponding elements. Like combining two sports scorecards into one summary.

slides.title: Matrix Multiplication
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak asks: if each run is worth 1 point, each wicket is worth 5 points penalty, and each boundary is worth 2 points, what's the total score for each match? Rohan multiplies matrices.

points.label: Rule
points.text: If A is m×n and B is n×p, then AB is m×p. Element (AB)_{ij} = Σ A_{ik} · B_{kj} (sum over k from 1 to n).

points.label: Important
points.text: Only works if columns of A = rows of B. Not commutative: AB ≠ BA usually.

points.label: Scalar multiplication
points.text: Multiply each element by a constant: k·A means multiply each a_{ij} by k.

example.problem: A = [[150, 160, 145]], weights = [[1], [5], [2]]. Find A × weights (score per match).

slides.inSimpleWords: Matrix multiplication combines data and weights. It's like calculating a weighted average, but organized in matrices.

slides.title: Determinant and Inverse
slides.storyContext: Simran introduces a 2×2 matrix from Rohan's data and explains the determinant (a special number derived from the matrix).

points.label: Determinant of 2×2
points.text: For A = [[a b], [c d]], det(A) = ad − bc.

points.label: Inverse
points.text: If det(A) ≠ 0, A has an inverse: A^{−1} = (1/det(A)) · [[d −b], [−c a]].

points.label: Key property
points.text: A · A^{−1} = I (identity matrix). Inverse only exists if determinant ≠ 0 (matrix is invertible).

slides.inSimpleWords: The determinant is a single number that tells you if a matrix can be inverted. Inverse reverses the matrix's operation.

slides.title: System of Linear Equations
slides.storyContext: Coach asks: if total runs across 2 matches is 300 and their difference is 10, how many runs in each? Rohan uses matrices to solve.

points.label: Matrix form
points.text: A · X = B, where A is coefficients, X is unknowns, B is constants.

points.label: Solution
points.text: X = A^{−1} · B (if A invertible).

example.problem: Solve x + y = 300; x − y = 10 using matrices.

slides.inSimpleWords: Write a system of equations in matrix form, find the inverse, multiply to solve for unknowns.

slides.title: Challenge: Tournament Scores
slides.storyContext: Rohan has scores from 2 tournaments (each 2×3 matrix: rows = Team A, B; columns = Match 1, 2, 3). He adds them, multiplies by a weights matrix to rank teams.

example.problem: Tournament 1 = [[150 160 145], [140 155 150]]. Tournament 2 = [[160 155 150], [145 160 155]]. Find total, then multiply by [[0.3], [0.3], [0.4]] to get weighted scores.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine matrices by addition, then multiply by weights to prioritize certain matches. Practical data science.

slides.title: What Rohan Learned
slides.storyContext: Matrices are Rohan's go-to tool for organizing and analyzing sports data.

points.text: Matrix: rectangular array of m rows and n columns. Element a_{ij} is row i, column j.
Operations: addition (element-wise), subtraction (element-wise), multiplication (combine columns of A with rows of B).
Transpose A^T swaps rows and columns. Matrix multiplication A·B is only defined if columns of A = rows of B.
Determinant = number derived from matrix; only non-zero determinants have inverses.
Inverse A^{−1}: A · A^{−1} = I. Used to solve systems of linear equations: A·X = B → X = A^{−1}·B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Matrices organize numbers. You add, multiply, and invert them like numbers — but element-wise or row-column paired. Powerful for real-world data.

subject: Mathematics
title: Zara's Area Mystery
hook: Zara uses determinants to calculate land areas from coordinates, uncovering geometry hidden in numbers.

slides.title: Determinants
slides.storyContext: Zara's father is a land surveyor. He has coordinates of a triangular plot but needs its area. Determinants transform coordinates into area instantly.

slides.title: The Land Survey
slides.storyContext: Zara's father has a triangle plot with vertices at (0, 0), (4, 0), (2, 3) in a Delhi suburb. He's marked these with GPS. He asks Zara: what's the area? Dr. Mehra says: determinants give you the answer without the distance formula.

slides.title: What is a Determinant?
slides.storyContext: Dr. Mehra explains: A determinant is a special number calculated from a square matrix. It encodes information about the matrix's invertibility and geometric scaling.

points.label: Notation
points.text: For a square matrix A, determinant is det(A) or |A|.

points.label: 2×2 determinant
points.text: For A = [[a b], [c d]], det(A) = ad − bc.

points.label: Geometric meaning (2×2)
points.text: det(A) is the signed area of the parallelogram formed by row vectors (or column vectors) of A.

example.problem: Find determinant of A = [[2 3], [1 4]].
example.solution: det(A) = 2·4 − 3·1 = 8 − 3 = 5. The parallelogram formed by [2, 3] and [1, 4] has area 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: A determinant is a number derived from a square matrix. For 2×2, it's ad − bc.

slides.title: 3×3 Determinant (Expansion)
slides.storyContext: For Zara's triangle area, she needs a 3×3 determinant. Dr. Mehra teaches expansion by minors.

points.label: Expansion along row 1
points.text: For A = [[a b c], [d e f], [g h i]], det(A) = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg).

points.label: Minor
points.text: M_{ij} = determinant of 2×2 matrix after removing row i and column j.

points.label: Cofactor
points.text: C_{ij} = (−1)^{i+j} · M_{ij}. Alternating signs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expand a 3×3 determinant by picking a row, then combine minors with alternating signs.

slides.title: Area of a Triangle from Coordinates
slides.storyContext: Zara's triangle has vertices A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(2, 3). Determinant gives area directly.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area = (1/2) · |det of [[x₁ y₁ 1], [x₂ y₂ 1], [x₃ y₃ 1]]|.

points.label: Why it works
points.text: The determinant of this augmented matrix (with 1s) scales the area of the triangle by 2. Absolute value ensures positive area.

example.problem: Find area of triangle with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (2,3).

slides.inSimpleWords: Plug triangle vertices into a 3×3 determinant formula, divide by 2, take absolute value — instant area.

image.alt: Area of a Triangle from Coordinates — Determinants

slides.title: Properties of Determinants
slides.storyContext: Dr. Mehra shares rules that make calculations faster. Zara uses these shortcuts.

points.label: If two rows are identical
points.text: det(A) = 0. No unique area — degenerate shape.

points.label: If two rows are swapped
points.text: det changes sign. Order matters geometrically.

points.label: If a row is multiplied by k
points.text: det is multiplied by k. Scaling one side scales area by k.

points.label: Multiplicative property
points.text: det(A·B) = det(A)·det(B).

points.label: det(A^T) = det(A)
points.text: Transpose doesn't change determinant.

slides.inSimpleWords: These properties help simplify calculation. Identical rows mean zero area (degenerate). Swapping rows flips the sign.

slides.title: Cramer's Rule
slides.storyContext: Zara learns a powerful method to solve systems of linear equations using determinants — no inverse needed.

points.label: For 2 equations
points.text: a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂. x = det([[c₁ b₁], [c₂ b₂]]) / det([[a₁ b₁], [a₂ b₂]]), y = det([[a₁ c₁], [a₂ c₂]]) / det([[a₁ b₁], [a₂ b₂]]).

points.label: General form
points.text: For system A·X = B, x_i = det(A_i) / det(A), where A_i is A with column i replaced by B.

points.label: Condition
points.text: Works only if det(A) ≠ 0 (unique solution exists).

example.problem: Solve 2x + 3y = 8 and x − y = 1 using Cramer's rule.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cramer's rule: replace columns one by one with the constants, calculate determinants, divide. Faster than matrix inverse for small systems.

slides.title: Collinearity Check
slides.storyContext: Zara's father marks three points on a map. Are they collinear (on a single line)? Determinant tells instantly.

points.label: Idea
points.text: Three points are collinear if and only if the area of the triangle they form is zero.

points.label: Method
points.text: Calculate det of [[x₁ y₁ 1], [x₂ y₂ 1], [x₃ y₃ 1]]. If det = 0, collinear.

example.problem: Are (1,2), (2,4), (3,6) collinear?

slides.inSimpleWords: If three points' determinant is zero, they're on the same line.

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-plot Calculation
slides.storyContext: Zara's father surveyed 2 adjacent triangular plots. Plot 1: (0,0), (5,0), (2,4). Plot 2: (5,0), (8,0), (6.5,4). Find both areas and total.

example.problem: Calculate areas using determinants and find total.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply the determinant area formula to each triangle separately, then sum.

slides.title: What Zara Learned
slides.storyContext: Determinants turned Zara into a math surveyor, solving land problems with elegance.

points.text: Determinant: a number from a square matrix. For 2×2: ad−bc.
3×3 determinant: expand by minors along a row, with alternating signs.
Geometric meaning: determinant = signed area (or volume in 3D) of parallelogram (or parallelepiped) formed by matrix rows/columns.
Triangle area = (1/2)|det([[x₁ y₁ 1], [x₂ y₂ 1], [x₃ y₃ 1]])|.
Cramer's rule: solve systems by replacing columns with constants, computing determinants, dividing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Determinants unlock geometry from coordinates. Instant areas, collinearity checks, system solutions.

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's River Run
hook: Priya's morning run along a river teaches her about smooth curves, sudden breaks, and rates of change.

slides.title: Continuity and Differentiability
slides.storyContext: Priya runs along the Yamuna River. Some stretches are smooth; some have sudden drops (a wall). She realizes: smooth paths have good derivatives, broken paths do not.

slides.title: The River Path
slides.storyContext: Priya's running path elevation: flat for 1 km, then slopes up 45° for 2 km, then flat again. But there's a barrier wall (sudden 2-meter drop) that interrupts the path. The smooth slopes have good tangent lines; the wall breaks continuity.

slides.title: What is Continuity?
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Singh defines: A function f is continuous at x=c if the curve doesn't jump or break at that point.

points.label: Three conditions (all required)
points.text: 1) f(c) is defined. 2) lim_{x→c} f(x) exists. 3) lim_{x→c} f(x) = f(c).

points.label: Geometric intuition
points.text: You can draw the curve without lifting your pen.

points.label: Discontinuity types
points.text: Removable (hole at a point), jump (sudden jump), infinite (asymptote).

example.problem: Is f(x) = {x² if x≠1; 2 if x=1} continuous at x=1?
example.solution: f(1) = 2. lim_{x→1} x² = 1. Since limit ≠ f(1), discontinuous (removable discontinuity — the hole at (1,1) is not filled correctly).

slides.inSimpleWords: Continuous = no jumps, holes, or breaks. The limit from both sides equals the function value at that point.

slides.title: Introduction to Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Dev asks Priya: how fast were you running at the 2 km mark? The answer is the derivative — instantaneous rate of change.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Derivative of f at x=c: f'(c) = lim_{h→0} (f(c+h)−f(c)) / h.

points.label: Geometric meaning
points.text: Slope of the tangent line to the curve at (c, f(c)).

points.label: Notation
points.text: f'(x), df/dx, Df(x) all mean the same thing.

example.problem: Find derivative of f(x) = x² at x=3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative = rate of change, or slope of tangent line. Measures how fast the function is increasing/decreasing at that point.

slides.title: Rules for Derivatives (Power, Product, Chain)
slides.storyContext: Computing derivatives by definition is slow. Mrs. Singh teaches shortcut rules.

points.label: Power rule
points.text: d/dx [x^n] = n·x^{n-1}.

points.label: Product rule
points.text: d/dx [u·v] = u'·v + u·v'.

points.label: Quotient rule
points.text: d/dx [u/v] = (u'·v − u·v') / v².

example.problem: Find derivative of f(x) = (3x² + 1)·sin(x).

slides.inSimpleWords: Power rule: power goes down, multiply. Product rule: first times derivative of second, plus second times derivative of first. Chain rule: derivative of outer times derivative of inner.

slides.title: Differentiability and Continuity
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Singh clarifies the relationship: If a function is differentiable (has a derivative), it must be continuous. But continuity doesn't guarantee differentiability.

points.label: Statement
points.text: If f is differentiable at x=c, then f is continuous at x=c.

points.label: Contrapositive
points.text: If f is discontinuous at x=c, then f is not differentiable at x=c.

points.label: Converse is false
points.text: f can be continuous but not differentiable. Example: f(x) = |x| at x=0 (sharp corner, no unique tangent).

example.problem: Is f(x) = |x| differentiable at x=0?
example.solution: f is continuous at 0: lim_{x→0} |x| = 0 = f(0). But: left derivative = lim_{h→0⁻} (−h) / h = −1. Right derivative = lim_{h→0⁺} h / h = 1. Left ≠ Right, so not differentiable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Smooth curve (differentiable) ⟹ connected curve (continuous). But connected doesn't mean smooth — corners exist.

slides.title: Left and Right Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Priya's path has a sharp turn at the barrier wall. Dev explains left and right derivatives.

points.label: Left derivative
points.text: f'₋(c) = lim_{h→0⁻} (f(c+h)−f(c)) / h. Slope from the left.

points.label: Right derivative
points.text: f'₊(c) = lim_{h→0⁺} (f(c+h)−f(c)) / h. Slope from the right.

points.label: Differentiable iff
points.text: f'₋(c) = f'₊(c) and both exist.

example.problem: For f(x) = |x−2|, find left and right derivatives at x=2.
example.solution: f'₋(2) = −1 (slope from left is −1). f'₊(2) = 1 (slope from right is 1). Not differentiable at x=2 (sharp corner).

slides.inSimpleWords: Smooth functions have equal left and right slopes. Sharp corners have different slopes from each side.

slides.title: Instantaneous Velocity Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya's position at time t (in hours) is s(t) = t² (distance in km). What is her instantaneous velocity at t=2?

points.label: Position function
points.text: s(t) = t².

example.problem: Find instantaneous velocity at t=2 hours.
example.solution: v(2) = 2(2) = 4 km/hour. At the 2-hour mark, Priya is running at 4 km/hour.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative of position gives velocity. Tells you speed at a specific instant.

slides.title: Challenge: Piecewise Continuity and Differentiability
slides.storyContext: Priya's path function: f(x) = {x² if x < 1; 2x − 1 if x ≥ 1}. Is it continuous and differentiable at x=1?

example.problem: Check continuity and differentiability at x=1.
example.solution: Continuity: f(1) = 2(1)−1 = 1. lim_{x→1⁻} x² = 1. lim_{x→1⁺} (2x−1) = 1. All equal, so continuous. Differentiability: f'₋(1) = 2(1) = 2 (derivative of x²). f'₊(1) = 2 (derivative of 2x−1). Both equal, so differentiable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check continuity at the junction (all pieces meet). Check if left and right derivatives match. If yes to both, smooth transition.

slides.title: What Priya Learned
slides.storyContext: Calculus explains the smoothness and speed of Priya's running path and any motion.

points.text: Continuity: no jumps, holes, or breaks. Three conditions: f(c) defined, limit exists, limit = f(c).
Derivative: instantaneous rate of change, slope of tangent line. f'(c) = lim_{h→0} (f(c+h)−f(c))/h.
Key rules: power, product, chain, quotient — shortcuts to compute derivatives without limits.
Differentiable ⟹ continuous. But continuous ≠ differentiable (corners break differentiability).
Sharp corners have unequal left/right derivatives. Smooth points have matching left/right derivatives.

slides.inSimpleWords: Continuous functions don't break. Differentiable functions are smooth. Derivatives measure instantaneous rate of change.

image.alt: What Priya Learned — Continuity and Differentiability

subject: Mathematics
title: Ananya's Business Optimization
hook: Ananya runs a small business making Indian snacks. Derivatives help her maximize profit and minimize waste.

slides.title: Application of Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Ananya's ladoo production factory gets x kilos of ghee per day. Profit depends on x. Too little ghee = low profit; too much = waste. Derivatives find the optimal x.

slides.title: The Ladoo Factory
slides.storyContext: Ananya's daily profit function: P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500 (x = kilos of ghee, P = profit in rupees). Vikram says: derivatives find the maximum profit point. Where should she buy exactly the right amount of ghee?

slides.title: Critical Points and Extrema
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair teaches: To find max/min, take the derivative, set it to zero, solve for x.

points.label: Critical point
points.text: Point where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) doesn't exist.

points.label: First Derivative Test
points.text: At x=c: if f' changes from + to −, it's a maximum. If − to +, it's a minimum. If no change, it's neither.

points.label: Second Derivative Test
points.text: If f''(c) > 0, c is a minimum. If f''(c) < 0, c is a maximum.

example.problem: Find max/min of P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500.

slides.inSimpleWords: Maximum = peak of a hill (derivative 0, second derivative negative). Minimum = valley (derivative 0, second derivative positive).

slides.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
slides.storyContext: Ananya checks: as x increases from 0, does profit grow or shrink? The sign of f'(x) tells.

points.label: f'(x) > 0
points.text: Function is increasing. Profit rises as ghee amount rises.

points.label: f'(x) < 0
points.text: Function is decreasing. Profit falls as ghee amount rises.

points.label: Finding intervals
points.text: Solve f'(x) = 0 to find critical points. Test signs of f' in each interval.

example.problem: For P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500, find where it's increasing and decreasing.
example.solution: P'(x) = −4x + 100. P'(x) = 0 at x=25. For x < 25: P'(x) > 0 (increasing). For x > 25: P'(x) < 0 (decreasing). Max profit at x=25.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative tells the direction: positive = up, negative = down, zero = flat (peak or valley).

slides.title: Concavity and Inflection Points
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair introduces curvature: Does the curve bend upward (concave up) or downward (concave down)?

points.label: f''(x) > 0
points.text: Concave up. Graph looks like ⌢ (minimum at critical point).

points.label: f''(x) < 0
points.text: Concave down. Graph looks like ⌣ (maximum at critical point).

points.label: Inflection point
points.text: Where f''(x) = 0 and changes sign. Curve changes concavity.

example.problem: For f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 2, find inflection points.
example.solution: f'(x) = 3x² − 6x. f''(x) = 6x − 6. Set f''(x) = 0: 6x − 6 = 0 ⟹ x = 1. f''(0) = −6 < 0 (concave down left). f''(2) = 6 > 0 (concave up right). Inflection at x=1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Second derivative tells curvature. Zero and sign change = inflection point (curve flips from cup to cap).

slides.title: Optimization in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Vikram shares business scenarios where derivatives solve practical problems.

points.label: Minimize cost
points.text: Find dimensions of a packaging box that minimizes material (surface area) for fixed volume.

points.label: Maximize revenue
points.text: Find the price/quantity that maximizes profit = revenue − cost.

points.label: Minimize time
points.text: Find the optimal speed to minimize travel time + fuel cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up function (cost, profit, time), take derivative, set to zero, solve. Second derivative confirms max or min.

slides.title: Box Optimization Problem
slides.storyContext: Ananya needs to ship ladoos in boxes. She has a rectangular sheet 20 cm × 30 cm. She'll cut squares of side x from corners, fold up, and tape. What x maximizes volume?

example.problem: Maximize V(x) = x(20−2x)(30−2x).

slides.inSimpleWords: Write volume in terms of x, find where derivative = 0, check which solution is in valid range, calculate max volume.

image.alt: Box Optimization Problem — Application of Derivatives

slides.title: Motion: Speed, Acceleration, Distance
slides.storyContext: Ananya's delivery bike position: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t (meters, t in seconds). What's instantaneous speed at t=2? Is the bike speeding up or slowing down?

points.label: Velocity = ds/dt
points.text: Speed at a moment.

points.label: Acceleration = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
points.text: How fast speed is changing.

example.problem: Find velocity and acceleration at t=2.
example.solution: v(t) = s'(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9. At t=2: v(2) = 12 − 24 + 9 = −3 m/s (moving backward). a(t) = v'(t) = 6t − 12. At t=2: a(2) = 12 − 12 = 0 m/s² (no acceleration at this instant).

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative of position = velocity. Derivative of velocity = acceleration. Second derivative of position = acceleration.

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-step Optimization
slides.storyContext: Ananya sells ladoos at price p rupees per box. Daily demand q = 500 − 10p boxes. Cost per box is 20 rupees. Find price p that maximizes profit.

example.problem: Profit = (revenue) − (cost) = (p·q) − (20·q). Find optimal p.

slides.inSimpleWords: Express profit as function of price/quantity, differentiate, set to zero, solve. Check second derivative for max/min.

slides.title: What Ananya Learned
slides.storyContext: Calculus turned Ananya into an optimizer, running her business with mathematical precision.

points.text: Critical points: f'(x) = 0. Find them to locate max/min.
First Derivative Test: derivative changes sign at critical point. + to − = max, − to + = min.
Second Derivative Test: f''(c) < 0 ⟹ max, f''(c) > 0 ⟹ min.
Concavity: f''(x) > 0 = concave up. f''(x) < 0 = concave down. Inflection = sign change of f''.
Real applications: optimize dimensions (volume, area), price (profit, revenue), motion (velocity, acceleration).

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives find where functions peak and valley. Critical business tool for profit, cost, and efficiency.

subject: Mathematics
title: Nikhil's Distance Challenge
hook: Nikhil's bike has a broken speedometer. He knows his speed over time but needs to find total distance traveled. Integration is his answer.

slides.title: Integrals
slides.storyContext: Nikhil's speedometer is broken, but his GPS logs speed v(t) every second. To find distance, he reverses differentiation — that's integration.

slides.title: The Broken Speedometer
slides.storyContext: Nikhil's data: v(t) = 20 − 2t m/s (speed decreasing linearly over time). He knows: distance = integral of speed. Ravi says: integration is the reverse of differentiation. If derivative of position gives velocity, integrating velocity gives position back.

slides.title: What is an Integral?
slides.storyContext: Ravi explains: An integral is the reverse of a derivative. If F'(x) = f(x), then ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C.

points.label: Antiderivative
points.text: F is an antiderivative of f if F'(x) = f(x).

points.label: Indefinite integral
points.text: ∫f(x)dx represents ALL antiderivatives: F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

points.label: Constant of integration
points.text: C accounts for the fact that derivative of constant is 0. Different antiderivatives differ by a constant.

example.problem: Find ∫ 3x² dx.
example.solution: We need F(x) such that F'(x) = 3x². F(x) = x³ works because (x³)' = 3x². So ∫ 3x² dx = x³ + C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integral = reverse of derivative. Antiderivative of f is any function whose derivative is f. Plus C because constants disappear in derivatives.

slides.title: Power Rule and Basic Integration
slides.storyContext: Ravi lists integration rules, starting with the most common.

points.label: Constant multiple
points.text: ∫ k·f(x) dx = k ∫ f(x) dx.

points.label: Sum rule
points.text: ∫ [f(x) + g(x)] dx = ∫ f(x) dx + ∫ g(x) dx.

points.label: Exponential and log
points.text: ∫ e^x dx = e^x + C. ∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C.

example.problem: Find ∫ (5x² + 2x − 3) dx.

slides.inSimpleWords: Power rule: bring exponent down, raise power by 1, divide by new exponent. Same linearity as derivatives.

slides.title: From Velocity to Distance
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma connects physics and math: if v(t) = 20 − 2t, then distance s(t) = ∫ v(t) dt.

points.label: Position from velocity
points.text: s(t) = ∫ v(t) dt. Integrating velocity gives position.

points.label: Finding C
points.text: Use initial condition. If Nikhil starts at s(0) = 0, then C = 0. So s(t) = 20t − t².

example.problem: Nikhil's speed v(t) = 20 − 2t m/s. He starts at position 0. Find position at t = 5 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integrate velocity to get position. Use initial position to find the constant C.

slides.title: Definite Integral and Area
slides.storyContext: Ravi introduces definite integrals: ∫ᵃᵇ f(x) dx gives the signed area under the curve from x=a to x=b.

points.label: Notation
points.text: ∫ᵃᵇ f(x) dx is the definite integral from a to b (limits of integration).

points.label: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
points.text: ∫ᵃᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is an antiderivative of f.

points.label: Geometric interpretation
points.text: If f(x) ≥ 0, the definite integral equals the area under the curve.

example.problem: Find ∫₀⁵ (20 − 2t) dt (distance traveled from t=0 to t=5).
example.solution: Antiderivative: F(t) = 20t − t². ∫₀⁵ (20−2t) dt = F(5) − F(0) = (100−25) − 0 = 75 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Definite integral has limits (a to b). Fundamental Theorem: evaluate antiderivative at b, subtract at a.

slides.title: Substitution Method (u-substitution)
slides.storyContext: Some integrals look complex. Ravi teaches substitution to simplify.

points.label: Idea
points.text: Let u = g(x). Then du = g'(x)dx. Rewrite integral in terms of u, integrate, substitute back.

points.label: Example
points.text: ∫ (2x)·cos(x²) dx. Let u = x², du = 2x dx. Then ∫ cos(u) du = sin(u) + C = sin(x²) + C.

example.problem: Find ∫ 3x² · sin(x³) dx.
example.solution: Let u = x³, du = 3x² dx. ∫ sin(u) du = −cos(u) + C = −cos(x³) + C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Substitution simplifies complex integrals. Replace inner function with u, find du, integrate, substitute back.

slides.title: Area Between Two Curves
slides.storyContext: Nikhil rides alongside his friend. Both their speeds vary over time. What's the total distance difference after 10 seconds?

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area between curves f(x) and g(x) (f ≥ g) from a to b: ∫ᵃᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx.

example.problem: Nikhil: v₁(t) = 20−2t. Friend: v₂(t) = 15−t. Find distance difference from t=0 to t=5 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Area between curves = definite integral of (upper curve − lower curve). Shows accumulated difference.

slides.title: Challenge: Complex Integration
slides.storyContext: Nikhil's actual speed is v(t) = 30·e^{−0.1t} m/s (exponential decay as he tires). Total distance after 10 seconds?

example.problem: Find s = ∫₀¹⁰ 30·e^{−0.1t} dt.

slides.inSimpleWords: For exponential integrals, use substitution or recall ∫ e^{ax} dx = (1/a)·e^{ax} + C.

slides.title: What Nikhil Learned
slides.storyContext: Integration reversed differentiation, turning speed data into distance — a practical superpower.

points.text: Integral = reverse of derivative. Antiderivative F satisfies F'(x) = f(x).
Indefinite integral: ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C (C = constant of integration).
Power rule: ∫ x^n dx = x^{n+1}/(n+1) + C.
Definite integral: ∫ᵃᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus).
Applications: distance from velocity, area under curves, area between curves, work, volume.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integration finds totals: distance from speed, area from height, accumulation from rate. Core tool for physics and engineering.
